paragraphs: Our Sages of blessed memory said: "It is a mitzvah to eat on the eve of Yom Kippur and to eat abundantly at the meal," and the Kabbalists of blessed memory wrote that one should eat an amount equivalent to two days, if a person is able to eat that much, in order to complete through eating on this day what is needed both for this day and for the morrow, which is the holy Yom Kippur; and a person should do all his deeds for the sake of Heaven, and the Blessed Name will not withhold good from those who walk in innocence. The later authorities of blessed memory wrote that it is a mitzvah to eat fish on the eve of Yom Kippur specifically in the morning, and there is some support for this from the Midrash - see "Mateh Ephraim"; and it appears that there is a reason for this, for fish allude to the "open, illuminated eye" which is the aspect of this day, in the secret of the verse "Joseph is a fruitful vine, a fruitful vine by a fountain (eye)" (Genesis 49:22), and "he who is good of eye shall be blessed."

clarification.explanation: It is a mitzvah to eat on the eve of Yom Kippur and to eat abundantly at the meal. The Kabbalists wrote that it is fitting to eat an amount equivalent to two days (if one is able), so as to complete through eating both this day and Yom Kippur itself, on which one does not eat; and one should do all this for the sake of Heaven. The later authorities wrote that it is a mitzvah to eat fish on the eve of Yom Kippur specifically in the morning (and there is a hint and support for this from the Midrash); and there is a reason for this custom - fish allude to the "open, illuminated eye," belonging to the sefirah of Yesod, which is the matter of this day, as hinted in the verse "Joseph is a fruitful vine, a fruitful vine by a fountain (eye)," and "he who is good of eye shall be blessed."
takeaways: It is a mitzvah to eat and to eat abundantly at the meal on the eve of Yom Kippur - even an amount equivalent to two days, if possible.
It is a mitzvah to eat fish on the morning of the eve of Yom Kippur.
The fish carry a kabbalistic hint: they symbolize the "open eye" belonging to Yesod, as hinted in the verse "Joseph is a fruitful vine... by a fountain (eye)."

paragraphs: In the circling of the kaparot he should have in mind the name Chet-Tav-Kaf, an acronym for: this is your exchange, your substitute, your atonement, and it is derived from the final letters of "You open Your hand" (Psalms 145:16); and for a female he should say "your exchange, your substitute, your atonement" with a tzeirei instead of a kamatz under the tav, as mentioned in "Mateh Ephraim." They circle it corresponding to the four forms of death imposed by the court, to atone for the person, and therefore a person must contemplate repentance at that time; and according to the secret, the matter of this slaughter is to sweeten the attribute of Gevurah, therefore the most fitting time for this is in the watch close to dawn, which is a time of favor. But here in our city, where there is the great community of the "fruitful son of Joseph," it is impossible to do everything at that hour, so the slaughterers of the city are compelled to begin this from the start of the night; and even though more than thirty slaughterers circulate throughout the city, they still cannot finish it all in one night, but complete it also in the first three or four hours of the day, trusting in the Lord that all will be accepted and rise as a favor before Him as if everything had been done properly.

clarification.explanation: In the circling of the kaparot he should have in mind the name Chet-Tav-Kaf (an acronym for 'this is your exchange, your substitute, your atonement,' and hinted in the final letters of 'You open Your hand'); and for a woman he should say 'your exchange, your substitute, your atonement' - with a tzeirei under the tav, and not with a kamatz and patach as in the masculine form. They circle it corresponding to the four forms of death imposed by the court, for atonement, and therefore one must contemplate repentance at that time. According to the secret, the slaughter sweetens the attribute of Gevurah, and therefore the most fitting time is the watch close to dawn (a time of favor); but in Baghdad, because of the large community, the slaughterers begin already from the start of the night and complete it also in the first hours of the day.
takeaways: In the kaparot one has in mind the name Chet-Tav-Kaf and contemplates repentance (corresponding to the four forms of death imposed by the court); for a female the vocalization changes - 'your exchange, your substitute, your atonement' with a tzeirei.
The most preferred time is close to dawn (a time of favor); because of the size of the community, they begin already at night.

paragraphs: Any householder to whose home the slaughterer comes to slaughter should not let him slaughter until he first checks the knife properly, and he should check it again after the slaughter; and the householder should have ashes from the hearth ready in his hand to slaughter into, and placing the earth first is the beginning of the mitzvah of covering the blood, therefore it is good for the householder himself to place the earth in his hand. The custom is that the householder recites the blessing over the covering of the blood, and the blessing is "Al kisui hadam be'afar" (on covering the blood with earth); and since there are many fowl to slaughter, the householder recites the blessing over the first one, and one of the household members over the second and third, and so on in this manner; and likewise the slaughterer himself also covers at the end. There is no excess of blessings here, since each person recites the blessing over a distinct slaughter and fresh blood. Also, they must have ready for the slaughterer a lamp with two wicks, with the wicks separated where the flame is, and only their flames touching together, so that he may slaughter by their light.

clarification.explanation: When the slaughterer comes to the home to slaughter the kaparot, they should not let him slaughter until he first checks the knife properly, and he should check it again after the slaughter. The householder should have ash or earth ready to slaughter into (this is the beginning of the mitzvah of covering the blood), and the custom is that the householder recites the blessing 'Al kisui hadam be'afar'; and since there are many fowl - the householder blesses over the first, and the household members over the following ones (each over a distinct slaughter and fresh blood). They should also have ready for the slaughterer a lamp with two wicks (separated where the flame is, but their flames touching) to slaughter by its light.
takeaways: Check the slaughterer's knife before the slaughter and after it; prepare earth for covering the blood.
The householder recites the blessing 'Al kisui hadam be'afar' (and household members over the following ones); provide the slaughterer with a two-wick lamp.

paragraphs: At the final meal before the fast, the custom in our house from ancient times is to dip the bread in sugar, and so wrote "Mateh Ephraim" regarding the custom of Ashkenaz; but one should also bring salt to the table and dip the bread in salt. And the custom in Ashkenaz is to say at the end of the final meal before the fast "A Song of Ascents: When the Lord brought back the captivity of Zion" (Psalms 126), as mentioned in "Magen Avraham," and there is a reason for this custom and it is correct to say it; and I have instituted here in our city, may God protect it, to say "A Psalm of Thanksgiving" in the morning service, as is the custom of the Chassidim in "Beit El" (may it be rebuilt and reestablished) in the Holy City, may it be rebuilt speedily.

clarification.explanation: At the final meal before the fast, it was customary in Rabbi Yosef Chaim's house to dip the bread in sugar (as is also the custom of Ashkenaz), but one should also bring salt to the table and dip the bread in it as well. In Ashkenaz they say at the end of the final meal before the fast 'A Song of Ascents: When the Lord brought back the captivity of Zion' (and it is correct to say it). And Rabbi Yosef Chaim instituted in his city to say 'A Psalm of Thanksgiving' in the morning service, as is the custom of the Chassidim of Beit El.
takeaways: At the final meal before the fast, one dips bread in sugar and also in salt.
One says 'A Song of Ascents: When the Lord brought back the captivity of Zion' at the end of the meal.

paragraphs: Regarding sins between a person and his fellow, Yom Kippur does not atone until he appeases him; therefore every person must ask forgiveness of his fellow on the eve of Yom Kippur, or earlier during the Ten Days of Repentance. And it is good for the cantor to announce before "Kol Nidrei": Gentlemen, forgive one another! And the congregation should say: We forgive! - so that at that hour an advocacy will be aroused above for Israel; a thing said in its proper time, how good it is. And so I have instituted, with the help of the Blessed Name, here in our city, may God protect it.

clarification.explanation: Regarding sins between a person and his fellow, Yom Kippur does not atone until he appeases his fellow; therefore every person must seek forgiveness from his fellow on the eve of Yom Kippur or earlier, during the Ten Days of Repentance. And it is good for the cantor to announce before 'Kol Nidrei': 'Gentlemen, forgive one another!' and the congregation should answer 'We forgive!' - so as to arouse advocacy for Israel.
takeaways: Yom Kippur does not atone for sins between a person and his fellow until he appeases him.
One asks forgiveness from others before the fast; and the cantor announces mutual forgiveness before Kol Nidrei.

paragraphs: Every person should kiss the hands of his father and mother on the eve of Yom Kippur toward evening, before going to the synagogue, and ask their forgiveness; and this is a great obligation upon every person, and one who does not do so is called a sinner who demeans the honor of his father and mother. For if regarding matters between a person and his fellow our Sages of blessed memory obligated seeking forgiveness before Yom Kippur, how much more so from one's father and mother, whom no person is free of sinning against every day. And if the son is foolish and did not ask, they should grant him forgiveness, saying with their mouths: I forgive my son so-and-so for all he has sinned against me, complete forgiveness. Likewise the husband should grant forgiveness to his wife for having wasted from the household against his will; and likewise any student who has a rabbi in his city should go to him before Yom Kippur and ask his forgiveness.

clarification.explanation: Every person should kiss the hands of his father and mother on the eve of Yom Kippur toward evening, before going to the synagogue, and ask their forgiveness - this is a great obligation; and one who does not do so is considered a sinner who demeans the honor of his parents (and how much more so than his fellow). And if the son is foolish and did not ask - they should say with their own mouths that they grant him complete forgiveness. Likewise the husband should forgive his wife for wasting from the household against his will, and any student who has a rabbi in the city should go to seek his forgiveness.
takeaways: One kisses the hands of one's parents and asks their forgiveness on the eve of Yom Kippur - a great obligation.
People forgive one another (husband to wife, parents to son), and a student asks forgiveness from his rabbi.

paragraphs: Women should be careful on the eve of Yom Kippur regarding the plucking of chickens, since they are many and lice known as "keeney or ha'of" (feather lice) are commonly found on them, attached to the skin of the fowl, and this matter is very common here in our city; and if a woman sees that the plucking is difficult due to their abundance, she should peel off the entire skin and discard it.

clarification.explanation: Women should be careful on the eve of Yom Kippur about cleaning chickens, since lice attached to the fowl's skin are commonly found. And if the cleaning is difficult due to their abundance - she should peel off the entire skin and discard it.
takeaways: Fowl should be carefully cleaned of lice before Yom Kippur; and if difficult, the entire skin should be removed.

paragraphs: One should be careful to immerse on the eve of Yom Kippur, and one who is prevented and unable to immerse in a mikveh should pour nine kabin, as I have written above in parashat Nitzavim in the laws of Rosh Hashanah. And women too should immerse on the eve of Yom Kippur for the sake of purity, and I have already written above in parashat Nitzavim the order of immersions; and men and women alike should do this on the eve of Yom Kippur. And see "Mateh Ephraim" siman 606 se'if katan 8, where he wrote: Even youths and maidens who have reached the age of mitzvot should immerse, and they should be scrupulous about interposition, and should perform the immersion after cutting their nails and combing their hair - see there.

clarification.explanation: One should be careful to immerse on the eve of Yom Kippur; and one who is prevented and unable to immerse in a mikveh should pour nine kabin (as explained in parashat Nitzavim in the laws of Rosh Hashanah). Women too immerse on the eve of Yom Kippur for purity, as do youths and maidens who have reached the age of mitzvot. One should be careful about interposition, and should perform the immersion after cutting nails and combing hair.
takeaways: One immerses in a mikveh on the eve of Yom Kippur (or pours nine kabin if prevented), both men and women.
One immerses after cutting nails and combing hair, and takes care regarding interposition.

paragraphs: Women light candles as on Friday night, and recite the blessing: "To light the candle of Yom Kippur"; and the custom of our city is that women recite "Shehecheyanu" over the candles of the festival and of Yom Kippur. And if it falls on Shabbat they bless: "To light the candle of Shabbat and Yom Kippur"; and once they have lit, the sanctity of Yom Kippur takes effect upon them and they are forbidden in labor and in all five afflictions.

clarification.explanation: Women light candles as on Friday night and recite the blessing 'To light the candle of Yom Kippur'; and the custom of Baghdad is that women also recite 'Shehecheyanu' over the candles of the festival and of Yom Kippur. And if it falls on Shabbat - they bless 'To light the candle of Shabbat and Yom Kippur.' And from the moment they light, the sanctity of Yom Kippur takes effect upon them and they are forbidden in labor and in the five afflictions.
takeaways: Women light the Yom Kippur candle and recite the blessing (and in Baghdad, also Shehecheyanu).
With the lighting, the sanctity of the day takes effect - prohibition of labor and the five afflictions.

paragraphs: The custom of the women in Ashkenaz is to prepare, on the eighth day of the month of Tishrei, the wicks for the candles of Yom Kippur, and for the candles carried to the synagogue to be lit for Yom Kippur, because that day is the first day of the dedication of the Holy Temple; and it is a beautiful custom.

clarification.explanation: The women of Ashkenaz were accustomed to prepare, on the eighth of Tishrei, the wicks for the Yom Kippur candles (and for the candles brought to the synagogue), because that day was the first day of the dedication of the Holy Temple; and it is a beautiful custom.
takeaways: The wicks for the Yom Kippur candles are prepared on the 8th of Tishrei (the first day of the Temple's dedication).

paragraphs: One should add from the mundane onto the holy; and on Friday night the acceptance is by the recitation of "Bo'i Kallah" and "A Psalm, a Song for the Sabbath Day," but on the night of Yom Kippur the addition takes effect through the blessing of "Shehecheyanu"; and if he explicitly accepted the addition with his mouth, it takes effect from the time of his acceptance. The custom is that the one holding the "Kol Nidrei" scroll recites the blessing "Shehecheyanu" aloud, and intends to discharge the obligation of the congregation with the blessing, and those listening should also intend to be discharged by his blessing; and if there is a person whose hearing is weak and cannot hear the blessing well, he should recite it for himself while the other is reciting it. The one reciting the blessing should first say twice, aloud, the verse "Light is sown for the righteous," and the congregation should say it with him quietly; and afterward he should say: "With the permission of my teacher and masters," and the congregation responds: "Heaven," meaning with the permission of Heaven. And I explained by way of hint, in the acronym of the word "Shamayim" (Heaven): Shome'a, Mashmi'a, Yachdav Mechavnim (the listener and the announcer intend together).

clarification.explanation: It is a mitzvah to add from the mundane onto the holy. On Friday night the acceptance is made through the recitation of 'Bo'i Kallah' and 'A Psalm, a Song for the Sabbath Day,' but on the night of Yom Kippur the addition takes effect through the blessing of 'Shehecheyanu' (and if he explicitly accepted it with his mouth, it takes effect from the time of his acceptance). The custom is that the one holding the 'Kol Nidrei' scroll recites 'Shehecheyanu' aloud and intends to discharge the congregation, and the listeners intend to be discharged (and one whose hearing is weak should recite it for himself). The one reciting the blessing first says twice, aloud, 'Light is sown for the righteous,' and afterward says 'With the permission of my teacher and masters,' and the congregation answers 'Heaven' (meaning with the permission of Heaven) - and there is a beautiful hint in the acronym of the word 'Shamayim' (Heaven): 'Shome'a, Mashmi'a, Yachdav Mechavnim' - meaning, the listener and the one making it heard intend together as one.
takeaways: On the night of Yom Kippur, the addition of sanctity is accepted through the blessing of 'Shehecheyanu.'
The one holding 'Kol Nidrei' recites Shehecheyanu aloud and discharges the congregation.
The congregation's response 'Shamayim' (Heaven) is hinted in the acronym 'Shome'a, Mashmi'a, Yachdav Mechavnim.'

paragraphs: A minor before the age of eleven should not fast; afterward, if he is able, he should fast. The obligation from the Torah is: a male of thirteen years and one day, and a female of twelve years and one day; and by rabbinic decree there is an obligation a year before that, to train them.

clarification.explanation: A minor under the age of eleven should not fast on Yom Kippur; from that age onward, if he is able, he should fast. The Torah obligation to fast is: a male of thirteen years and one day, and a female of twelve years and one day; and by rabbinic decree there is a (partial) obligation a year earlier, in order to train them.
takeaways: A minor under eleven does not fast; above that age, according to his ability.
Full obligation: a male of thirteen years and a day, a female of twelve years and a day (with training a year earlier).

paragraphs: Even if it falls on a weekday, one should not say the verse "Vehu Rachum"; rather one should say: "Ki Kel Rachum...", "Hashem Tzeva'ot imanu...", "Hashem Tzeva'ot ashrei...", "Hashem hoshi'ah..."; and the reason is as written in the holy Zohar, parashat Terumah, page 130, regarding Shabbat - see there. And all the more so on Yom Kippur, which contains the illumination of Binah, and even the Satan has no permission to accuse - certainly one should not say it; and Yom Kippur should not, God forbid, be lesser than the other festivals, on which it is not said. And one should not rely in this matter on the book "Chemdat Yamim" regarding this holy day, which is the choicest ("chemdat") of all the days of the year.

clarification.explanation: Even if Yom Kippur falls on a weekday - one does not say the verse 'Vehu Rachum,' but rather says 'Ki Kel Rachum' etc. The reason is according to the Zohar (as on Shabbat), and all the more so on Yom Kippur, which contains the illumination of Binah, and even the Satan has no permission to accuse. And one should not rely in this matter on the book 'Chemdat Yamim' regarding this holy day.
takeaways: On Yom Kippur (even on a weekday) one does not say 'Vehu Rachum,' but rather 'Ki Kel Rachum.'

paragraphs: One should be careful not to place a vessel of drinking water beside his bed on the night of Yom Kippur, even though water is needed for giving the young children to drink; rather he should place it far away, for one must be concerned lest he rise from his sleep very thirsty and forget that it is Yom Kippur and drink, God forbid. And it is permitted to swallow saliva on Yom Kippur, though some are stringent; and one who is able should be careful about this.

clarification.explanation: One should be careful not to place a vessel of drinking water near his bed on the night of Yom Kippur (even though water is needed to give the young children to drink), but should place it far away - lest he rise thirsty, forget that it is Yom Kippur, and drink. And it is permitted to swallow saliva on Yom Kippur; some are stringent, and one who is able should be careful.
takeaways: Do not place drinking water beside the bed at night, lest one drink out of forgetfulness.
It is permitted to swallow saliva (though some are stringent).

paragraphs: He should not touch his wife, whether at night or during the day, as in the laws of a niddah; and some say that only at night is it forbidden to touch, but during the day there is no concern, and for some need one may rely on those who permit it during the day. And they should also be careful that husband and wife not sleep in one bed, even though each has his own separate bedding.

clarification.explanation: He should not touch his wife - whether at night or during the day - as in the laws of a niddah. Some say that only at night is touching forbidden, but during the day there is no concern, and for some need one may rely on those who permit it during the day. And they should also be careful that husband and wife not sleep in one bed, even though each has his own separate bedding.
takeaways: One does not touch his wife on Yom Kippur as in the laws of a niddah (some are lenient during the day, for a need).
Husband and wife do not sleep in one bed, even with separate bedding.

paragraphs: Even though there are those who permit touching foods on Yom Kippur, as mentioned in the gloss on the Shulchan Aruch, nevertheless there are those who forbid it. Therefore specifically a woman who needs to do so, who is compelled to touch food in order to give it to her child and the like, may then rely on those who are lenient; but any other person who has no great need to touch should be careful.

clarification.explanation: Even though some permit touching foods on Yom Kippur, others forbid it; therefore only a woman who is compelled to touch food (in order to give it to her child, and the like) may rely on the lenient opinion, but any other person who has no great need should be careful not to touch.
takeaways: Avoid touching food on Yom Kippur; a woman who needs to do so (to feed a child) may be lenient.

paragraphs: "And honor it, the holy of the Lord" (Isaiah 58:13) - this is Yom Kippur; honor it with clean clothing. And our Sages of blessed memory said: One makes up the bed, and on the table one spreads a beautiful cloth as on Shabbat; and every person should be careful not to touch his shoes, for even though they are made of cloth, his hands become impure from them. And the blessing "Who has provided me with all my needs" is not recited on Yom Kippur, because everyone goes barefoot.

clarification.explanation: "And honor it, the holy of the Lord" - this is Yom Kippur; honor it with clean clothing. And the Sages said one makes up the bed, and spreads a beautiful cloth on the table, as on Shabbat. And one should be careful not to touch his shoes - for even though they are of cloth, they render the hands impure. And the blessing "Who has provided me with all my needs" is not recited on Yom Kippur, because everyone is barefoot.
takeaways: Honor the day with clean clothing, a made-up bed, and a beautiful tablecloth, as on Shabbat.
One does not touch one's shoes, and does not recite the blessing "Who has provided me with all my needs."

paragraphs: One should pray with weeping all the prayers of Yom Kippur, which are: Shacharit, Minchah, Ma'ariv, Musaf, and Ne'ilah, and the Selichot and the confessions; and if he cannot bring down tears, he should say them in a weeping voice, as it is said: "For the Lord has heard the voice of my weeping" (Psalms 6:9). And before the Torah reading one should be aroused to weeping over the death of the sons of Aaron the Kohen, peace be upon him, and this weeping is capable of serving as a crown. And every person should be careful to arrange the prayer and the Selichot to himself before Yom Kippur, so that he can have proper intent for what he utters with his mouth, for this day is holy to our God, and everything follows the intentions of the heart. And one must also say the text of "Al Chet" in the order of Tav-Shin-Resh-Kof (reversed), which is in the secret of the returning light, as mentioned in the siddur of our Rabbi the Rashash of blessed memory, and so wrote the Gaon Chida of blessed memory in "Birkei Yosef." And at the time of the confession he should strike his heart literally, and with most people one finds the heart beneath the breasts, about four fingers down; and one should be careful about this whenever reciting confession throughout the days of the year.

clarification.explanation: One should pray all the prayers of Yom Kippur with weeping (Shacharit, Minchah, Ma'ariv, Musaf, Ne'ilah, Selichot, and the confessions); one who cannot bring down tears should say them in a weeping voice. Before the Torah reading one should be aroused to weeping over the death of the sons of Aaron. And every person should arrange the prayer and Selichot for himself before Yom Kippur, so as to have proper intent. "Al Chet" should also be said according to the reversed order of the letters (from the end of the alphabet to its beginning, Tav-Shin-Resh-Kof) - an order that hints, according to the secret, at the "returning light" - and at the time of confession one strikes the heart literally (located about four fingers beneath the chest), and one should be careful about this also when reciting confession throughout the rest of the year.
takeaways: All the prayers of Yom Kippur are recited with weeping, and one who cannot bring down tears should weep aloud.
Before the Torah reading, one is aroused to weeping over the death of the sons of Aaron.
"Al Chet" is also said in the reversed order of letters (Tav-Shin-Resh-Kof), hinting, according to the secret, at the "returning light."
At the time of confession one strikes the heart literally (about four fingers beneath the chest), throughout the whole year and not only on Yom Kippur.

paragraphs: One should say the Thirteen Attributes slowly, with intent and with a broken heart, and this is the essential thing; and some pious ones, when saying the Thirteen Attributes, count them on their fingers, in the manner done when reciting the eleven ingredients of "the balsam and the onycha," and it is a beautiful custom, for through this the intent is aroused, and there is also in this an endearment of the mitzvah.

clarification.explanation: One says the Thirteen Attributes slowly, with intent and a broken heart - and this is the essential thing. Some pious ones count them on their fingers (as is done when reciting the eleven ingredients of the incense), and it is a beautiful custom, arousing intent and containing an endearment of the mitzvah.
takeaways: The Thirteen Attributes are said slowly and with a broken heart.
Some count them on their fingers to arouse intent.

paragraphs: Even when Yom Kippur falls on a weekday, the crown of the heads, the Gaon our master, my grandfather Rabbi Moshe Chaim, may his memory be for a blessing, instituted here in the city of Baghdad to say "Et Musafei" in the plural form; see "Chikrei Lev," Orach Chaim, page 97, what he wrote about this.

clarification.explanation: Even when Yom Kippur falls on a weekday, the grandfather of Rabbi Yosef Chaim (Rabbi Moshe Chaim) instituted in Baghdad to say "Et Musafei" in the plural form.
takeaways: In Baghdad they say "Et Musafei" in the plural form even when Yom Kippur falls on a weekday.

paragraphs: On Yom Kippur one should study in Ezekiel from the beginning of chapter 40 to the end of chapter 43, where there is the prophecy that the prophet Ezekiel, peace be upon him, prophesied about the Third Temple, on Yom Kippur itself, as it is written: "In the beginning of the year, on the tenth of the month" (Ezekiel 40:1) - meaning the beginning of the Yovel (Jubilee) year. And our Rabbis of blessed memory said in the Midrash: The Holy One, blessed be He, said to the prophet Ezekiel, peace be upon him: Let Israel study your prophecy about the form of the House, and I will credit it to them as though they were engaged in its building - until here.

clarification.explanation: On Yom Kippur one should study in Ezekiel from the beginning of chapter 40 to the end of chapter 43 - the prophecy Ezekiel prophesied about the Third Temple, on Yom Kippur itself ("In the beginning of the year, on the tenth of the month," which is the beginning of the Yovel year). And it is said in the Midrash that the Holy One, blessed be He, said to Ezekiel: Let Israel study the prophecy of the form of the House, and I will credit it to them as though they were engaged in its building.
takeaways: On Yom Kippur one studies Ezekiel chapters 40-43 (the prophecy of the Third Temple).
Studying the form of the House is considered as though one were engaged in its building.

paragraphs: The explanation of "Raise Your right hand and cause my redemption to sprout" - the intent is regarding the birth of the "Yechidah" for the King Messiah; and what is written "Reveal Your might upon us" is in the manner of what the verse says: "Stir up Your might, and come to save us" (Psalms 80:3). And some are scrupulous to say "Reveal Your might and redeem us," and so I am accustomed, for a person must phrase his words as supplications, in the manner of what our teacher Rabbi Chaim Vital of blessed memory wrote regarding what is written "and good hope," and what is written "bring forth our judgment to light," meaning by kindness which is called "light." And in the recitation of "Do it for the sake of Abraham, Your perfect native son," which is said in the Selichot, one should add on Yom Kippur, in all the Selichot of all the prayers, to say: "Do it for the sake of Your servant Rabbi Akiva ben Yosef, who was killed for the sanctification of Your name," and this should be said before saying "Do it for the sake of those killed and burned..."

clarification.explanation: The explanation of "Raise Your right hand and cause my redemption to sprout" - the intent is regarding the birth of the "Yechidah" for the King Messiah; and "Reveal Your might upon us" is like the matter of "Stir up Your might, and come to save us." Some are scrupulous to say "Reveal Your might and redeem us" (and so is the custom of the Ben Ish Chai), for a person must phrase his words as supplications (as Rabbi Chaim Vital wrote regarding "and good hope" and regarding "bring forth our judgment to light" - meaning, by the kindness called "light"). And in the recitation of "Do it for the sake of Abraham, Your perfect native son" in the Selichot - on Yom Kippur one adds, in all the Selichot of all the prayers, to say: "Do it for the sake of Your servant Rabbi Akiva ben Yosef, who was killed for the sanctification of Your name," saying this before "Do it for the sake of those killed and burned."
takeaways: "Raise Your right hand and cause my redemption to sprout" refers to the birth of the "Yechidah" for the King Messiah; and it is proper to say "Reveal Your might and redeem us" (a phrasing of supplication).
On Yom Kippur one adds in the Selichot: "Do it for the sake of Rabbi Akiva ben Yosef, who was killed for the sanctification of Your name," before "Do it for the sake of those killed and burned."

paragraphs: After eating the meal that breaks the fast, on the night after Yom Kippur, one should say at the table the "Opening of Elijah," of blessed memory, and Rabbi Yaavetz of blessed memory wrote to study in the Ra'aya Meheimna, parashat Emor, page 99, side b: "The day of Rosh Hashanah is a day of judgment, etc.," until page 100: "Fortunate is their portion in this world and in the World to Come." And afterward he should recite the final blessing over his meal, and rise promptly to make some preparation for the sukkah.

clarification.explanation: After the meal that breaks the fast on the night after Yom Kippur, one says at the table the "Opening of Elijah," and studies in the Ra'aya Meheimna, parashat Emor (page 99b to page 100) - "The day of Rosh Hashanah is a day of judgment," etc. Afterward he recites the final blessing over his meal, and rises promptly to make some preparation for the sukkah.
takeaways: On the night after Yom Kippur one says the "Opening of Elijah" and studies in the Ra'aya Meheimna.
One rises promptly to begin preparing for the sukkah.
